International Criminal Court · Trial Chamber III · No. ICC‑01/21‑01/25 Prosecutor v. Duterte A former president of the Philippines, charged at the International Criminal Court with three counts of crimes against humanity. The prosecution says he and the people around him had a plan to kill people accused of drug crimes and other crimes, first through a death squad in Davao City and then through police and others across the country. His defense has said there was no such plan and that nothing ties him to the deaths. He has been held in The Hague since March 2025, and judges have refused to end the case, to release him, or to find him unfit for trial. The trial is set to open on November 30, 2026, and nothing has been proved yet. Arrested Mar 11, 2025 Before Korner, Paek, Guillou Trial opens Nov 30, 2026 Status Undecided

Prosecution The side bringing the charges The court’s own prosecution office At this court a case is brought in the name of the Prosecutor, the same way a criminal case in the US is brought in the name of the People or the State. The Prosecutor’s office is part of the court but it works on its own, so it isn’t acting for any country here, and that includes the Philippines. The person running this case is the deputy prosecutor, Mame Mandiaye Niang. The chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, isn’t on it. Appeals judges took him off in October 2025, because before he got the job he had worked for victims of these same killings and they said that could look like bias. The ruling was about how it could look, and it didn’t find that he was biased. ICC, case information sheet · Record 286-Red, p. 18

Defendant The person charged President of the Philippines, 2016–2022 He was born in 1945 and grew up in Davao, on the southern island of Mindanao. He trained as a lawyer and spent nine years as a prosecutor for the city before he went into politics there in 1986. He was mayor of Davao City for more than 22 years in all, and the tough-on-crime name he made there is what he ran on for president in 2016. He won, served the one six-year term a president gets, and left office in 2022. In May 2025, two months after his arrest, Davao elected him mayor again. One of his sons has been doing the job in his place, and his daughter Sara is the country’s vice president. The court calls him the accused. Record 417-Red ¶¶ 78–79 · Record 282-Red ¶ 51 · Background: Britannica · Reporting: GMA News, Jul 1, 2025
Notes Record reviewed through November 8, 2026 . Nothing filed after that date is reflected here.
How this was made, and what it leaves out

Built from the court’s own public record of the case, which held 577 documents on November 8, 2026. These pages rest on the decisions, the charges, each side’s main filings and the transcripts of ten hearings, and not on a reading of every annex. Every characterization here comes from a filing, a transcript or a signed decision, and each side is quoted from its own filings and its own lawyers. Every record number in a citation opens that document in the ICC Legal Tools Database, an open online library that carries the court’s public records. Citations to a page open the document at that page.

A great deal. Most filings exist twice, a confidential version and a public one with parts redacted, and these pages can only read the public one. In the charges that takes out the names of all but five of the 78 people and the dates and places of most of the 49 incidents. Nearly every witness is only a number, like P-0002. The medical findings about him are blacked out, and so is the country he asked to be released to. His lawyer at the time told the judges the redactions were “so sweeping that virtually nothing intelligible remains of the 49 incidents” for the public to read. The presiding judge answered that the defense sees all of it, and that “it just is not available to the public.” Record 178-Red2 ¶¶ 27–77 · Tr. T-007, 44:17–20, 52:5–7

Victims are named here only where the public charges name them, which is five people. The charges also name eight officials the prosecution says shared the plan with him. None of the eight is on trial in this case, and the judges wrote that what they said about those eight is not a finding about anyone’s guilt but his. The charges covered 78 people, and in October 2026 the trial judges let in seven more incidents. The prosecution calls that a fraction. The Philippine government’s own count of people killed in police anti-drug operations from July 2016 to February 2019 was 5,281, and the estimates the court cited when it opened the investigation ran from 12,000 to 30,000. A wider number is used on these pages only with whose number it is. Record 417-Red ¶ 85 · Record 519-Red ¶ 47 · Record 12 ¶¶ 39, 67

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. Judges have said twice that there is enough here to go on, once to order his arrest and once at the confirmation of charges, and both times the test was lower than proof. A conviction takes proof beyond reasonable doubt. No witness has testified yet, and his lawyer told the court in February 2026 that he maintains his innocence. The two sides have formally agreed on four facts so far: when and where he was born, his nationality, what the initials PRRD stand for, and what a barangay is. Everything else is in dispute. Where the record doesn’t reach, these pages say so and stop. Tr. T-004, 38:17 · Record 259-Red ¶ 3

A permanent court in The Hague, in the Netherlands, that tries individual people for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. It is not part of the United Nations, and it only has power where its treaty gives it power.
The head of the court’s Office of the Prosecutor, which investigates and brings cases on its own authority. Every case here is titled in the Prosecutor’s name.

A panel of judges. A Pre-Trial Chamber of three handles a case up to the decision to send it to trial, a Trial Chamber of three hears the trial, and the Appeals Chamber of five hears appeals. There is no jury.
What this court calls the person on trial once the charges are confirmed. Before that the word is suspect.
How a filing is cited. ICC-01/21-01/25-417 is the 417th document in this case, shortened here to Record 417. “Red” on the end means it is the public version with parts blacked out.
Blacked out. Most filings here exist in a confidential version and a public one with names, dates or places removed, usually to protect witnesses and victims.
The word-for-word record of a hearing. Cited by page and line, so 9:14 means page 9, line 14.
Certain acts, murder among them, when they are part of a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population, carried out under a government’s or an organization’s policy.
One charge. This case has three.
One of the specific killings or attempted killings the prosecution lists as an example under a count.
The stage where three judges decide whether the prosecution has enough to justify a trial. It is a filter, and it is not a verdict.

How sure the judges have to be. Reasonable grounds to believe is enough for an arrest warrant. Substantial grounds to believe is enough to send a case to trial. A conviction takes proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Where it stands Waiting for the trial, which opens on November 30, 2026. The three questions that could have stopped it earlier have all been answered against him. If no If yes If no If yes If no If yes If no If yes If yes If no
Can this court hear the case at all?
The Philippines left the court in 2019

Had to be settled before anything else Yes · final since Apr 22, 2026 This is a question about jurisdiction, which just means the court’s power to hear a case. The court only has power where a country has joined its treaty. The Philippines joined in 2011 and then left, and the leaving took effect on March 17, 2019. The judges didn’t approve an investigation until 2021, which is more than two years after that. So his lawyers said the court had no power left by the time it acted, and that everything done since should be undone. It came down to one sentence in the treaty, which says that leaving doesn’t stop the court from carrying on with any matter it was already considering. The prosecutor’s office had started a preliminary examination, which is basically a first look, in February 2018. That was before the country left. The judges said that first look counts, so the court kept its power over what happened while the Philippines was still a member. The appeals judges agreed in April 2026, four to one. That makes this a yes, and it can’t be argued again.

Outcome Then The case ends and he goes home If the judges had gone the other way, the court would have had no power to try him, and nothing else on this page would matter. His lawyers asked for exactly that, along with his immediate release. It wouldn’t have been a finding that he did nothing. It would have been a finding that this court isn’t the one that gets to decide. One of the five appeals judges would have ruled this way. He wrote that a year was enough time for the prosecutor to get an investigation approved before the country was out.
Is he fit to stand trial?

Asked twice, and it can be asked again Yes · last decided Sept 28, 2026 Fitness is about whether he can actually take part in his own trial. It doesn’t mean healthy. It means he can understand what he’s charged with, follow what is said in court, and tell his lawyers what he wants them to do. He was 80 when his lawyers raised it in 2025. They said his memory and thinking had declined so much that the case should be put off with no end date. The judges had three independent doctors examine him, and then had the same three do it again before trial. Both times the doctors said he could do those things, and both times the judges agreed, first in January 2026 and then in September 2026. He is physically frail, so the court is making adjustments, like hearing support, a nurse at the breaks, and shorter days if he needs them. This one isn’t closed for good the way the first question is. If his health really changes, his lawyers can ask again.

Outcome Then The trial is put on hold If the judges found he couldn’t follow the trial or instruct his lawyers, the trial would be adjourned, which means postponed. That isn’t an acquittal and it doesn’t end the case. The court would look at it again every few months, and if he got better the trial would go ahead. If he never did, there would be no verdict either way. This is what his lawyers asked for in August 2025.
Is there enough to send it to trial?

A filter, and not a verdict Yes · all three counts, Apr 23, 2026 Before anyone goes on trial at this court, three judges have to check that the prosecution has enough to justify one. That step is the confirmation of charges. The prosecution doesn’t have to prove the case at this point. It only has to show substantial grounds to believe he committed the crimes, which is a lot lower than what a conviction takes. No witnesses came in for this one. The judges read the written evidence and heard four days of argument. His lawyers argued that the evidence was hearsay from admitted killers, that his speeches were bluster, and that nothing tied him to any of the deaths. The judges said those are arguments about who to believe, and that sorting that out is what a trial is for. On April 23, 2026, all three judges confirmed all three counts. That’s the reason there is a trial. It isn’t a finding that he did it.

Outcome Then No trial on them If the judges had found the evidence too thin, they would have declined to confirm the charges, or some of them, and there would be no trial on those. His lawyers asked for all of them to be thrown out and for him to be sent back to his family. That still wouldn’t be the same as being found not guilty. The prosecution could come back later with more evidence and ask again.

The case is here What has to be proved first Not yet heard From here on the test is the hard one. The prosecution has to prove everything beyond reasonable doubt, and he doesn’t have to prove anything. Three judges decide, and there is no jury. They’re supposed to try for a verdict all three agree on, and if they can’t get there, two out of three is enough. There are three counts, and each one gets its own answer. One is about killings in Davao City while he was mayor. One is about people on a list of high-value targets. One is about police operations in neighborhoods. For any of them, the first thing to prove is that a crime against humanity happened at all. That takes two things, and they’re the two cards inside this one. A no on either means not guilty on that count, and the judges never get to the question of him. Who must prove it The prosecution, all of it. That’s the burden of proof, and it stays on the prosecution from the first witness to the last. Both are needed and

Disputed This is about the specific deaths. There are 56 incidents now, because in October 2026 the trial judges let in seven more than the 49 that were confirmed. Neither side says these people didn’t die. The fight is over how. For a lot of them there is a police report saying officers went to make an arrest or a buy-bust, the person pulled a gun, and the police shot back. The word for that in the Philippines is nanlaban, which means fought back. If that’s what happened, it isn’t murder. The prosecution says the reports were written to cover the killings and that guns and drugs were planted, and it has former police officers and gunmen who say so. The defense says those witnesses are admitted killers, and that the reports are the only records made at the time and nothing shows they’re fake. Some of the deaths aren’t police operations at all, like the Davao killings and the two men shot inside a jail. Each incident gets looked at separately.
Were they part of an attack on civilians, carried out as policy?

Disputed A murder by itself isn’t something this court handles. What makes it a crime against humanity is that it was part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians, and that the attack carried out the policy of a government or an organization. So the prosecution has to prove there was a campaign to kill people accused of drug crimes and other crimes, that it was big enough or organized enough to count, and that it was policy and not just something that happened. A lot of this comes down to one word. The police order that started the national campaign talked about neutralizing drug suspects. The prosecution says everyone involved understood that to mean kill, and that there were cash rewards for killings. The defense says it means arrest or subdue, that the word was in police manuals before he was president, and that his speeches kept telling police to shoot only in self-defense. The defense also says that where a killing was unlawful, it was individual officers acting for their own reasons, and that isn’t a policy.

Outcome Then The other counts carry on The three counts are separate, so this isn’t all or nothing. If the judges aren’t sure the Davao killings were part of an organized attack, for example, count one fails and counts two and three carry on. A count that fails here never reaches the question of what he did or what he knew.

Where the defense has put most of its weight Not yet heard This is the question the defense has fought hardest. He isn’t accused of pulling a trigger. He’s accused of being the person at the top, as mayor and then as president. So even if the judges find the killings were murder and part of an attack, the prosecution still has to tie them to him. It also has to prove what was in his head, meaning that he meant for the killings to happen and knew about the wider attack. The charges give three different ways he could be responsible, and they’re the three cards inside this one. The prosecution only needs one of them to hold up for a count. His lawyer at the February 2026 hearing said there is “absolutely nothing to directly link” him to the deaths. The lawyers who argued that have since been replaced, and the new team hasn’t set out its case yet. Its first written statement was due on October 30, 2026, and it hasn’t been made public. A yes on any one is enough or or
Was there a plan to kill, and did he control the people who did it?
Route one · With and through others

Disputed This is the main one, and the law’s name for it is indirect co-perpetration. The prosecution has to show three things. One, that he and others had a common plan that was going to lead to killings. Two, that his part in it was essential, so the plan wouldn’t have worked without him. Three, that he and the others controlled the people who did the actual killing, so that when the word came down it got done. The prosecution says the plan started in Davao with the Davao Death Squad, and went national when he became president and put people from Davao in charge of the police and other agencies. It points out that the two times he pulled the police off the campaign, the killings dropped, and says that shows control. The defense says there was no plan and that the squad is a fiction. It says only about one in twenty of the people on the target list ended up marked “neutralized,” and that a plan to kill wouldn’t look like that.
Did he order the killings, or push people into them?

Disputed This route doesn’t need a shared plan. It asks if he used his authority to tell people to kill, or said things that prompted them to. Ordering doesn’t have to be in writing, and the judges who confirmed the charges said so. The prosecution leans on his public speeches here, like the promises to protect police who killed, and on the lists of names he read out, some of them people who were killed afterward. The defense says nobody has produced an order from him, and that not one of the prosecution’s inside witnesses heard him give one. The prosecution answers that one witness heard the order for a Davao killing come from him over the phone. The defense also says his speeches were rough talk meant to scare criminals, and that a politician saying violent things isn’t the same as a killing being his doing.
Did he help or encourage them, on purpose?

Disputed This is the fallback, and it asks the least of the three. Aiding and abetting means helping or encouraging a crime that somebody else commits, in order to make it easier. Here that could be the promises of protection and pardons, the rewards, or the people he appointed. He wouldn’t have to be the one in charge for this to apply. It still needs proof that he meant to help with killings, and not just with policing. The defense’s answer is the same as on the other two routes. It says what he backed was lawful police work and that he kept saying so in public.

Outcome Then A sentence, and then an appeal A conviction on any count leads to a separate sentencing stage. This court can give up to 30 years, or life in the most extreme cases, and it has no death penalty. The time he has already spent in detention would count toward the sentence. After that the judges can order reparations for victims. He could appeal both the conviction and the sentence to the five appeals judges.

Outcome Then Released, if it is every count If none of the three routes is proved for a count, he is acquitted on it. If that happens on all three counts, he is released. The prosecution can appeal an acquittal at this court, which isn’t how it works in the US. An acquittal would mean the prosecution didn’t prove its case to the standard a criminal court needs. It wouldn’t be a ruling on everything that happened in the Philippines in those years.

Read as a whole, he has lost every ruling that could have stopped the case before trial: on the court’s power, on his detention, and on his fitness. What he has won is narrower. The chief prosecutor was removed, the hearing on the charges was delayed five months for medical exams, and one incident was struck. None of it goes to whether the charges are true. That question has not been heard yet.
What the charges are about. The court can try only what happened while the Philippines was a member, and these are those years.
The court’s treaty takes effect for the Philippines

The country had ratified it two months earlier. From this day the court can try crimes committed on its soil, and the charges start on this date. The treaty is the Rome Statute. The Philippines ratified it on August 30, 2011, and it came into force for the country on November 1. He was vice mayor of Davao City at the time, with his daughter as mayor, and had been the mayor himself for most of the years since 1988. The prosecution says a death squad had been working in the city since the late 1980s. The court can’t reach anything from before this date, so the charges begin here. Record 309 ¶ 1 · Record 417-Red ¶ 78 · Record 178-Red2 ¶ 1

The first count is about nine incidents in these years, in which 19 people were killed. The prosecution says the Davao Death Squad did it and that he ran it. Only one of the nine has a date and place the public can read: December 4, 2013, in or around the Agdao Public Market. The names are blacked out. The prosecution says the people killed were accused of selling drugs or of theft, and that the squad needed his “green light” before it killed anyone. His lawyer at the 2026 hearing called the squad “that fictitious construct.” The judges who confirmed the charges found substantial grounds to believe that he recruited police officers and hired gunmen into it in the late 1980s. That is a lower test than proof. Record 178-Red2 ¶ 25, p. 11 · Tr. T-004, 11:7–10, 39:7 · Record 417-Red ¶ 87

The next day the national police open an anti-drug campaign called Project Double Barrel. The prosecution says this is when the plan from Davao went national. In the campaign he had said that if he won he would order the police and the military to hunt down drug lords “and kill them,” a line the prosecution read to the judges. The police order that set up Double Barrel spoke of “neutralizing” drug suspects. What that word meant is one of the main fights in the case. The prosecution says it meant kill. The defense says it meant arrest or subdue, and that it was ordinary police vocabulary from before his time. Record 417-Red ¶¶ 88, 54 · Tr. T-004, 10:15 · Tr. T-006, 25:2–16, 26:16–21
The killings in counts two and three

Forty incidents and 59 people, across the country. Count two is about people on a list of “high-value targets.” Count three is about police operations in neighborhoods. Five of the 59 are named in the public charges. Rolando Espinosa Sr. and Raul Yap were shot in a jail in Leyte on or about November 5, 2016. Reynaldo Parojinog Sr., the mayor of Ozamiz City, was killed with others early on July 30, 2017. Benjamin Visda was killed in Manila in October 2016. Kian Loyd delos Santos, who was 17, was killed in Caloocan City on or about August 16, 2017. The police reports on many of these deaths say the person fired first. The prosecution says those reports were falsified and that guns were planted. The defense says they are the only records made at the time and that nothing shows they are false. Record 178-Red2 pp. 12–14 · Tr. T-007, 11:1–15 · Tr. T-007, 20:15–22
The Prosecutor opens a first look

Fatou Bensouda, the chief prosecutor at the time, announces a preliminary examination of the killings. It isn’t an investigation yet. A preliminary examination is the prosecutor’s office checking whether there is enough to ask for a real investigation. No judge is involved at this point. Seven years later the whole question of whether the court can hear this case comes down to whether this step counted as the court already “considering” the matter. Record 309 ¶ 2
The Philippines gives notice that it is leaving

Five weeks after the first look is announced. Under the treaty a withdrawal takes one year to count. He was president when the notice was given. The prosecution later told the judges he pulled the country out when he thought he might be prosecuted. His lawyers say it is the prosecution that has to answer for not opening an investigation inside that year. Record 309 ¶¶ 3, 36 · Tr. T-007, 25:19–22

Mar 17, 2019 The withdrawal takes effect The Philippines is out of the court from this day, so the charges stop on March 16. Everything he is charged with happened above this line. Whether the court could still open a case about it from below the line is what his lawyers argued all the way to the appeals judges.
Asked for two years after the country left, paused when its government objected, and restarted.
The Prosecutor asks to open an investigation

Three years after the first look began, and two years after the Philippines left. When a prosecutor starts an investigation on their own, three judges have to approve it first. The request covered killings from November 1, 2011, to March 16, 2019, in Davao and then across the country. It was made public on June 14, 2021. Record 7-Red · ICC, case information sheet

Three judges find a reasonable basis to investigate the “war on drugs” killings and the earlier ones in Davao. The decision said the court kept its power over crimes committed while the country was a member, even though it had since left. It gave the government’s own count of people killed in police anti-drug operations as 5,281 by February 2019, and cited estimates of 12,000 to 30,000 in all. Record 12 p. 41, ¶¶ 39, 67, 111
The Philippines asks the court to step back

The government says it is looking into the killings itself. The Prosecutor pauses his work. The court is meant to step in only when a country isn’t genuinely investigating or prosecuting the crimes itself. A country can ask for a deferral, which means the Prosecutor stands back in favor of its own investigation. The Prosecutor told the judges on November 18 that he had temporarily suspended his work while he looked at the request. Record 14 ¶¶ 1–3

Karim Khan, now the chief prosecutor, tells the judges the deferral isn’t warranted. His term as president ended six days later, on June 30, 2022. The Philippine government filed its objections that September. Record 46 · Record 417-Red ¶ 79 · Record 51

The judges are not satisfied that the Philippines is carrying out real investigations that cover the same ground. In their words, they were “not satisfied that the Philippines is undertaking relevant investigations, or is making a real or genuine effort to carry out such investigations.” The government appealed a week later. Record 56-Red pp. 41–42
The Philippines loses its appeal, 3 to 2

Five appeals judges let the investigation go on. Two of them would have ended it because the country had already left. The government argued, among other things, that the court had no power over the Philippines once the withdrawal took effect. The majority said that point had not been properly raised and did not decide it. Judges Perrin de Brichambaut and Lordkipanidze dissented. They would have found that the court “cannot exercise its jurisdiction,” because the investigation was only asked for after the withdrawal. His own lawyers made the same argument two years later. Record 77 p. 4, ¶ 60 · Record 77-OPI · Tr. T-001
He tells the Senate he had a death squad

At an inquiry committee of the Philippine Senate. The prosecution says he said it under oath, three times. The judges who later confirmed the charges wrote that the evidence about the squad was “consistent with Mr Duterte’s admission in October 2024, before an inquiry committee of the Senate of the Philippines, that he had an organised death squad in Davao City.” The prosecution played the hearings in court. His lawyer’s answer to the things he has said in public was that they were “hyperbole, bluster and rhetoric.” Record 417-Red ¶ 87 · Tr. T-007, 26:7–9 · Tr. T-004, 34:18
From a secret warrant to a courtroom in The Hague in seven days.
The Prosecutor asks for an arrest warrant

For murder, torture and rape as crimes against humanity. Filed in secret. The application set out five counts covering 45 acts of murder, four of torture and three of rape. A redacted copy was made public on March 13, 2025, the day before he first appeared in court. Record 80-Red p. 22 · Record 90 ¶ 4

Three judges find reasonable grounds to believe he is responsible for at least 43 killings. They leave out torture and rape. The judges said the material was enough on the torture and the rape themselves, but that the link between those acts and the wider attack was “insufficiently shown.” The warrant covered at least 19 people killed by the Davao Death Squad and at least 24 killed by or under the supervision of police. They found an arrest was needed because he “appears to continue to wield considerable power.” The warrant was issued as secret and made public on March 11. Record 83 ¶¶ 12, 14, 26 · ICC, case information sheet

Philippine authorities arrest him on the court’s warrant. He is flown to the Netherlands and handed to the court on March 12. The court has no police of its own, so it depends on countries to make arrests and to surrender the person. Here it was the Philippine government, under the president who followed him. His lawyer told the judges three days later that the plane had waited more than five hours in the United Arab Emirates on the way, and called the whole transfer “a pure and simple kidnapping.” ICC, case information sheet · Record 90 ¶ 6 · Tr. T-002, 7:8–23

He appears on a screen from the detention center, gives his name and date of birth, and hears the charge read. The judges set the next hearing for September 23. It took 25 minutes. The presiding judge said the hearing was “neither the start of the trial, nor is it a confirmation of charges hearing.” He attended by video because the court’s doctors advised against bringing him in after the journey. The lawyer in the room for him was Salvador Medialdea, who had been his executive secretary. He asked for a week’s delay and was refused. Four days later Nicholas Kaufman took over as lead counsel. Tr. T-002, 4:3–6, 9:1–5, 10:8–11 · Record 92-Red
Through 2025 his lawyers ask the judges to end the case, to release him, and to find him unfit for trial. The charges are filed in the middle of it.
The defense says the court has no power here

The Philippines had left by the time judges opened the investigation in 2021, so there was nothing for the court to act on. This is a challenge to jurisdiction, and it is about timing. The treaty says a country leaving doesn’t stop the court from carrying on with “any matter which was already under consideration by the Court” before the withdrawal took effect. The defense says a prosecutor’s first look is too informal to count, and that “the Court” means the judges, who were not asked for anything until 2021. It asked for every step in the case to be undone. The prosecution answered that a preliminary examination is exactly such a matter. The victims’ lawyers called the treaty’s wording “crystal clear.” Record 121 ¶¶ 116–117 · Record 146-Red-Corr · Record 145 ¶ 1

While he is held in The Hague. One of his sons, elected vice mayor, does the job in his place. The judges later counted the result against him when he asked to be released. They wrote that the “continued support in the Philippines to Mr Duterte is further demonstrated by his election as mayor of Davao City in May 2025.” Record 282-Red ¶ 51 · Reporting: GMA News, Jul 1, 2025
He asks to be released while he waits

To a country whose name is blacked out, “under any conditions.” His lawyers say a man of 80 in poor health is not going to run. The request for interim release offered a list of conditions and made a humanitarian case. The prosecution opposed it. It said he “does not accept the legitimacy of the legal proceedings against him” and has the reach to get at witnesses. In July the defense asked the judges to hold off ruling while it gathered medical evidence, and two of the three agreed. It filed a renewed request with medical reports on August 18. Record 150-Red p. 16 · Record 159-Red p. 4 · Record 209 · Record 231-Red

Three counts of crimes against humanity. Forty-nine incidents and 78 people, which the prosecution calls a sample of something much larger. Count one is the murder of 19 people in or around Davao City by the Davao Death Squad. Count two is the murder of 14 “high-value targets” in 2016 and 2017. Count three is the murder of 43 people and the attempted murder of two more in barangay police operations through 2018. The document says he is responsible in any of three ways: by committing the crimes with and through other people under a common plan, by ordering or inducing them, or by aiding them. It names eight officials as sharing the plan. The public first saw a blacked-out copy on September 22, 2025. Record 178-Red2 ¶¶ 4, 19, 25, p. 16
The defense moves to take the chief prosecutor off the case

Before Karim Khan was the Prosecutor, he had worked for victims of the same killings. The request was for his disqualification. In 2018, in private practice and without a fee, he had worked on a submission to the Prosecutor of the day about the Philippine killings. The defense said a prosecutor who had acted for victims of these events could not now be the one bringing the case over them. Record 226-Red2 · Record 286-Red p. 3
The defense says he is not fit to stand trial

It asks for the case to be put off with no end date, saying his memory and thinking have declined. The filing opens: he “is not fit to stand trial as a result of cognitive impairment in multiple domains.” Fitness means being able to understand the proceedings and to instruct your lawyers. The prosecution and the victims’ lawyers both opposed an open-ended delay. The prosecution accepted a short one so that doctors could examine him. Record 230-Red ¶ 1 · Record 253-Red · Record 257-Red2

Prosecution No. The 49 incidents were always “a non-exhaustive list of examples.” The confirmed charges fix the period, the places and the groups involved, and the trial brief gives notice of the rest. Defense Yes. The charges are “a moving target” built on illustrative incidents under broad headings, with eight more added three months before trial “with no judicial oversight.” Victims’ lawyers The first motion should be thrown out, because it re-argues how the charges were confirmed, which the defense already lost. Court Mostly against the defense. On October 9, 2026, the trial judges refused to send the charges back and let in seven of the eight new incidents. They struck one for falling outside the dates of its count. Record 498 ¶ 2 · Record 519-Red ¶¶ 30, 37, 44, 47, 51 · Record 445 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument A case about a campaign of this scale cannot list every killing, and it doesn’t have to. What a defendant is entitled to is notice of the case in time to prepare, and the charges, the brief and the witness lists together give it. Complaints about the form of the charges belonged at the confirmation stage, where the defense made them and lost. Rests on Its December 2025 clarification that the incidents are examples. The confirmation decision, which accepted that. The trial brief, where the added incidents are set out. Record 330 ¶ 5 · Record 417-Red ¶¶ 22–24 · Record 499 · Record 504-Corr-Red Authority The confirmation decision itself, and Appeals Chamber rulings that notice can be given through documents like a trial brief. Where it is weak It did reach too far once. One added incident fell outside the period the prosecution had set for its own count, and the judges said it “cannot now be permitted to broaden the temporal scope.” They also said they “might have expected formal notice” by a written motion. Defense The argument A person on trial has to know the case he must meet. Charges framed around “illustrative non-exhaustive incidents, grouped under topical headings” let the prosecution reach for any killing in a country of 120 million over seven and a half years. Haynes told the judges that would make the trial “a sort of public enquiry” in which “our investigations will be impossible.” Rests on The wording of the charges. The notice of eight more incidents on August 31, 2026. The remedy asked for: an order that the prosecution re-file “an exhaustive list” of the acts charged. Record 487 ¶¶ 1–2, 21 · Record 502-Red ¶¶ 1–3 · Tr. T-009, 27:25–28:5 Authority The right to be told the charges in detail, the rule that changing charges after confirmation needs a judge’s leave, and the rule that a verdict cannot go beyond the facts charged. Where it is weak The same argument failed at confirmation and again when the defense asked for leave to appeal. The trial judges held they have no power to order confirmed charges redrawn. What the defense won was the removal of one incident. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Do the charges, read with the trial brief, tell him clearly enough what he has to answer? Defense A list that can keep growing is not a charge. It asks for the charges to be redrawn as a closed list. Prosecution The period, the places and the groups are fixed. Incidents inside those limits are examples of one charge. The eight added incidents They fall inside counts that were already confirmed, and the brief gave notice. The eight added incidents Adding them is changing the charges, and that needs a judge’s leave. Where it lands Seven in and one out. The trial covers 56 incidents. Witnesses on the new ones wait until the defense has had “reasonable time to prepare.”
Was the evidence handed over in a state the defense can use?

Prosecution Yes. Most of the volume is one set of police records of the deaths, which it was obliged to hand over. It has given the defense its own index to it, and a cap on evidence would be arbitrary. Defense No. In disclosure it got 62,130 items, about 57,000 of them since June, and fewer than 5,000 contain his name even once. It asks for the file to be cut to about 10,000. Court Undecided. The motion was filed on September 25, 2026, and no ruling was on the public record on November 8. Record 507-Red · Record 510-Red · Record 516-Red Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument The volume is reasonable for a case about thousands of deaths. One data set makes up 44,495 of the items, and it is the local police records of killings in anti-drug operations, which go to both the charged incidents and the wider attack. How often a search word turns up “is in no way indicative of the relevance of evidence.” Rests on Its own index of the data set, “the product of many hundreds of hours,” which it shared. A chart of summaries linking documents to each death. Meetings and metadata fixes for stray pages. Other cases with evidence lists of similar size. Record 510-Red ¶¶ 2–3, 5, 14, 18, 20 Authority The duty of disclosure itself, which obliges it to hand over what is relevant to the defense as well as what it will use. Where it is weak It accepts there are real stray pages and says it is fixing them. The summaries it offers as a guide were written by software. It disclosed 5,275 items before the charges were confirmed and has more than 19,000 on its list of evidence now, after the presiding judge had said “we don’t expect to be drowned in documents.” Record 510-Red ¶ 24 · Tr. T-009, 48:25 Defense The argument A record of that size, in that condition, eight weeks before trial, cannot be read, let alone tested. The complaint is about usability and not only volume: wrong labels, single loose pages, scans nobody can read, missing translations, duplicates. The defense says the big data set was put into the record “without meaningful review.” Rests on The counts in its motion: a 978 percent rise in disclosed items, more than 320,000 pages, and a 400-page document disclosed one page at a time. Record 507-Red ¶ 2, ¶ 10 · Record 516-Red ¶¶ 1–3 Authority The right to adequate time and facilities to prepare a defense. Where it is weak It is not asking for a later trial date, so the remedy it wants is a cap, and the prosecution says no defense team in comparable cases asked for one. Counting how often a name appears does not measure relevance. The prosecution says the defense has known about the data set since the first status conference and changed its position on receiving it. Record 510-Red ¶¶ 12, 16, 18 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Has the defense been given the evidence in time, and in a form it can actually work through before November 30? Defense Sixty-two thousand items, most of them since June, many mislabeled or unreadable. Prosecution Seven in ten of those are one set of police death records, indexed and shared. The remedy Leave the record as it is. A cap would force relevant evidence out. The remedy Order a new, smaller record of about 10,000 items. Where it lands Nowhere yet. The judges have not ruled, and the trial date has not moved.

Prosecution Yes. The Prosecutor said no conflict arose from “briefly representing a group of victims” in 2018, and that the request to remove him rested on “speculative” personal attacks. Defense No. The man who ran it had earlier acted for victims and treated Mr. Duterte as a suspect from 2018. His lawyers called the charges “politically motivated,” brought with help from the government that followed his. Court Split. Appeals judges took the chief prosecutor off the case in October 2025 for a reasonable appearance of bias, and found no actual bias. The case itself was left standing. Record 286-Red pp. 15, 18 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument Helping a group of victims file one submission, years before taking office, is not a conflict, and the defense’s own lawyer first thought so too. If the appeals judges saw it differently he would step away, and he did. The evidence stands or falls on what it shows, and the office found and disclosed statements that help the defense. Rests on The Prosecutor’s written response. The disclosure of interviews with people who denied wrongdoing, which the prosecution points to as the opposite of a one-track inquiry. Record 234-Red ¶¶ 1–3 · Tr. T-007, 25:3–15 Authority The Rome Statute’s rule on when a prosecutor must step aside, which the prosecution read as setting a high bar. Where it is weak The appeals judges did not accept its view of how this looked. They called his earlier involvement “significantly intense and multifaceted” and noted that people connected to it are now prosecution witnesses. Record 286-Red pp. 16–18 Defense The argument The investigation was “contaminated” by “a one-track crusade” toward a result fixed in advance. Three insiders were interviewed before the investigation lawfully resumed in 2023, while it was supposed to be paused. Removing the chief prosecutor came “too late in the day to salvage the integrity of the investigation.” Behind it all, the defense said, the president who followed him “set out to neutralise Rodrigo Duterte and his legacy.” Rests on The 2018 submission he signed as a private lawyer. The early interviews. The account of how witnesses were recruited. Record 226-Red2 · Tr. T-004, 31:14–15, 39:1–41:10 · Tr. T-006, 49:7–22 Authority The Prosecutor’s duty to look into circumstances that clear a suspect as carefully as those that incriminate him. Where it is weak It won the removal and asked for nothing more. The judges who confirmed the charges noted the defense raised the fairness of the investigation only in its opening remarks, did not “seek any relief,” and so they did not rule on it. The removal decision found no actual bias and did not touch the evidence. A motive for the case, political or not, does not answer what the evidence shows. Record 417-Red fn. 65 · Record 286-Red p. 15 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Could a fair-minded observer think the person in charge had already made up his mind? Defense He acted for victims of these same killings in 2018 and later ran the investigation into them. Prosecution One brief piece of work years earlier. The evidence was gathered by an office, not one man. What follows from it He steps aside and the case continues under his deputy. What follows from it The whole investigation is tainted and cannot be saved by removing him. Where it lands He was removed. No finding of actual bias, and no ruling that the investigation was unfair.
Is he fit to stand trial?

Prosecution Yes. It never accepted the defense doctors’ conclusions, agreed only to a short delay for an independent examination, and relies on the court’s own panel, which found him capable twice. Defense No. He “is not fit to stand trial as a result of cognitive impairment in multiple domains,” his condition “will not improve,” and he “suffers from significant memory impairment.” Victims’ lawyers An open-ended halt “is not justified.” The judges should appoint independent experts to examine him instead. Court Decided against the defense twice, on January 26 and September 28, 2026. It can be raised again if his health changes. Record 257-Red2 ¶¶ 3–4 · Record 356-Red p. 25 · Record 509-Red p. 17, ¶ 44 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument A case cannot be put off forever on the strength of reports from doctors hired by one side. Have independent experts examine him, decide quickly, and adjust the trial to what he needs. Being old and frail is not the same as being unable to take part. Rests on The court-appointed panel of three, which reported in December 2025 and again in August 2026 that he can understand the charges, follow the proceedings and instruct his lawyers. Record 253-Red ¶¶ 1–3 · Record 509-Red ¶¶ 19–23 Authority Fitness is a legal question that “does not depend, in and of itself, on whether the suspect has particular medical conditions.” Where it is weak The medical findings are blacked out, so the public cannot weigh them. The panel itself could not rule out “some mild or pre-clinical process,” and its members did not all agree on a diagnosis, though they agreed on what he is able to do. He is 81 and the trial is expected to be long. Record 356-Red ¶ 20 · Record 509-Red ¶¶ 19, 21 Defense The argument He cannot retain what happened recently, so he cannot follow evidence from day to day or give his lawyers real instructions. That won’t get better, and no adjustment to the timetable fixes it. The judges should at least hear the experts in person and allow more testing before deciding. Rests on Reports from doctors the defense retained in 2025. His scores on the panel’s own tests. What his lawyers say they see when they meet him. Record 230-Red ¶ 1 · Record 509-Red ¶ 25 · Record 383 ¶¶ 4–5 Authority The court’s rule that a trial must be adjourned if the accused is unfit. Where it is weak The defense itself accepted that he “understands the nature of the criminal process” and “the concept of the charge of murder.” The panel was unanimous on his capacities both times. It “expressed reservations” about his test scores, citing inconsistencies and underperformance for which it found no medical explanation. Record 356-Red ¶ 37 · Record 509-Red ¶¶ 22–23 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Can he understand the charges, follow the proceedings and instruct his lawyers? Defense Not with a memory that cannot hold on to recent information. Prosecution Three independent experts say he can, and said so twice. What the tests show Low scores that the experts doubted, with inconsistencies they could not explain medically. What the tests show Significant cognitive impairment, measured on the panel’s own tests. Where it lands Fit, with adjustments: hearing support, a nurse at breaks, hours decided as the trial goes. Open to review on a substantiated request.
Should he be held while he waits?

Prosecution Yes. It “strongly opposes” release. He “does not accept the legitimacy of the legal proceedings against him” and has the reach to flee or to get at witnesses. Defense No. He is past 80 and in poor health. A country whose name is blacked out agreed to take him, and he asked to be released there “under any conditions” the judges chose. Victims’ lawyers By saying he does not recognize the court and was kidnapped, he “has clearly demonstrated that he will abscond.” Court Refused on September 26, 2025, upheld unanimously on appeal, and kept in place at three reviews since. Tr. T-007, 57:7–11 · Record 282-Red p. 23 · Record 326-Red p. 3 · Records 357-Red, 447, 506 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument All three risks the law names are present. He rejects the court’s authority, so he has every reason not to come back. He has contacts and support, including family in high office. Witnesses in the Philippines are within reach of people loyal to him. Rests on His camp’s description of the arrest as a kidnapping. His daughter’s office as vice president. His election as mayor of Davao City while in custody. A son’s position of power at one of the places named in the charges. Record 159-Red ¶ 1, p. 4 · Record 252-Red ¶¶ 1–2 · Record 282-Red ¶¶ 50–53, 59 Authority The Rome Statute’s test for detention: a risk of flight, of obstructing the case, or of further crimes. Any one is enough. Where it is weak The risks are predictions. The test is “the possibility, not the inevitability, of a future occurrence,” and the judges said they did not need to find that he “has actually taken steps to contact or exercise pressure on potential witnesses.” The defense also says the prosecution had at first told it that it would not oppose release to a member country on agreed terms. Record 282-Red ¶¶ 52, 54 · Record 150-Red ¶ 3 Defense The argument He “is not a flight risk.” A government has agreed in principle to receive him and to enforce whatever conditions the judges set, and he would not embarrass his hosts by breaking them. He will not interfere with the case or commit crimes, the charged events are more than six years old, and his age and health are humanitarian reasons to let him out. Rests on The receiving government’s agreement, as the defense reported it. The terms and conditions it offered. Medical reports filed with the renewed request in August 2025. Record 150-Red ¶¶ 1, 5, p. 16 · Record 231-Red Authority The Rome Statute’s article on release, under which a person is let out unless one of the three risks is shown. Where it is weak Words used on his behalf became evidence against release. The judges counted his election and his family’s offices as signs of a network that could help him run. They also held that “the issue of fitness to stand trial is factually and legally distinct from the question of interim release,” so poor health did not answer the risks. Record 282-Red ¶¶ 51, 64 · Record 326-Red p. 3 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is detention needed to make sure he appears, to protect the case, or to prevent further crimes? Defense His age and health remove any real risk, and conditions can cover the rest. Prosecution He calls the arrest a kidnapping. A man who rejects the court has no reason to return to it. His standing at home Political contacts and family in office are a way out and a way to reach witnesses. His standing at home Being elected by his city is not a reason to keep a man in a cell. Where it lands Detained since March 12, 2025. Reviewed in January, May and September 2026, and kept in custody each time.
Can this court hear the case at all?

Prosecution Yes. The treaty stops a country from taking a matter out of the court’s hands by leaving, and the examination opened in February 2018 was such a matter. Defense No. This is a challenge to jurisdiction. A country has to be a member when the court uses its power, and the Philippines had been out for two and a half years when judges opened the investigation. Victims’ lawyers The treaty’s wording is “crystal clear,” and the Philippines handing him over in 2025 is “irrefutable proof” that it still accepts the court’s power. Court Decided for the prosecution, and final. Pre-trial judges ruled on October 23, 2025, and the Appeals Chamber on April 22, 2026, with one judge dissenting in part. Record 145 pp. 3, 15 · Record 309 p. 32 · Record 415 pp. 5–6 · Record 415-OPI Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument The treaty has a rule made for exactly this. A withdrawal “shall not prejudice in any way the continued consideration of any matter which was already under consideration by the Court” before it took effect. The prosecutor’s first look began 13 months before the Philippines was out. Otherwise a country could take a matter out of the court’s hands just by leaving. Rests on The dates. The text of the treaty’s article on leaving. The 2021 decision that opened the investigation, which already said the court kept its power over crimes from the membership years. Record 146-Red-Corr · Record 328 · Record 12 ¶ 111 Authority Article 127(2) of the Rome Statute. Where it is weak The judges agreed with the defense that ordinarily a country must be a member at the moment the court’s power is used. Two different appeals judges, across the 2023 and 2026 appeals, read the treaty the defense’s way. And the prosecutor’s office took more than three years to move from its first look to asking for an investigation. Record 309 ¶ 80 · Record 77-OPI · Record 415-OPI pp. 2–3 Defense The argument The article on the court’s power is written in the present tense. A country has to be a party at the moment that power is exercised, and that happened in 2021. The saving rule speaks of matters before “the Court,” which means the judges, and a prosecutor’s informal first look is not that. “The ‘fight against impunity’ cannot warrant an inappropriate application” of the treaty. If the prosecutor ran out of time, that is the prosecutor’s responsibility. Rests on The same dates. The wording of the two articles. The 2023 dissent by two appeals judges. Record 121 ¶¶ 116–117 · Record 171-Red · Record 319 · Record 309 ¶ 36 Authority Article 12(2) of the Rome Statute, read with article 13. Where it is weak It lost at both levels and the question is closed. The saving rule says “any matter,” which is hard to read narrowly, and it does not name a stage a matter has to have reached. The Philippine government itself carried out the arrest in 2025. Record 309 ¶¶ 76–77, 84 · Record 415 pp. 5–6 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Was this matter already “under consideration by the Court” before March 17, 2019? If a first look counts It began on February 8, 2018, so the court kept its power. If only judges count Nothing reached a judge until May 2021, so there was nothing to keep. Prosecution “Any matter” is broad on purpose, and a preliminary examination is a step the treaty itself sets up. Defense The court’s power is exercised by judges. A prosecutor reading reports is not the court considering anything. Where it lands Resolved for the prosecution. The Appeals Chamber held that a preliminary examination “qualifies as a ‘matter under consideration.’” The trial goes ahead on that footing.
